summary: Extends OSPF to define independent IP topologies called Multi-Topologies. They can compute different paths for unicast, multicast, different classes of service, or an in-band management topology. An optional extension can exclude selected links. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: OSPF computes one set of shortest paths, using one metric per link. Sometimes a network needs more than one: a fast path for some traffic and a cheaper path for other traffic, each computed over a different set of links. This RFC adds that to OSPF. It reuses the TOS field that OSPF already has, so no new packet format is needed, and it keeps several topologies side by side, each with its own metric and its own routing table.

subtitle: Running several independent sets of OSPF paths side by side, one metric and one routing table each.

tldr.problem: OSPF computes one set of shortest paths, with one metric per link. A network sometimes needs more: a fast path for some traffic and a cheaper path for other traffic, each computed over a different set of links.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC redefines the TOS field in OSPF link state advertisements as a Multi-Topology ID and uses it to carry a separate metric for each topology. A router then computes one shortest path tree per topology, and its routing table entries are per topology.
tldr.outcome: The change needs no new packet format, so it can be introduced gradually: MT routers live alongside non-MT routers in the default topology. A separate capability, DefaultExclusionCapability, allows particular links to be held out of the default topology once every router in the area supports it.

today: RFC 4915 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2007, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the specification of Multi-Topology routing in OSPF, with the optional extension that excludes links from the default topology.

sections.title: Why Reuse the Old TOS Field
sections.content:
OSPF uses a fixed packet format, therefore it is not easy to introduce any backward-compatible extensions. However, the OSPF specification introduced a Type of Service metric in an earlier specification in order to announce a different link cost based on TOS. TOS-based routing as described there was never deployed and was subsequently deprecated. A similar mechanism is described for IS-IS.

The proposal in this document is to reuse the TOS-based metric fields. They have been redefined and are used to advertise different topologies by advertising separate metrics for each of them.

Multi-Topology routing differs from TOS-based routing in three ways. With TOS routing, the TOS or Diffserv Code Point in the IP header was mapped directly to the corresponding OSPF SPF calculation and routing table, which limited the number and definition of the topologies to the 16 TOS values; with Multi-Topology routing, the classification of what type of traffic maps to which topology is not within the scope of the document. With TOS routing, traffic that was unreachable in the routing table associated with the corresponding TOS reverted to the TOS 0 routing table; with Multi-Topology routing this is optional. With TOS routing, individual links or prefixes could not be excluded from a topology: if the Link State Advertisement options T-bit was set, all links or prefixes were either advertised explicitly or defaulted to the TOS 0 metric; with Multi-Topology routing, links or prefixes that are not advertised for a specific topology do not exist in that topology.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPF uses a fixed packet format, so it is not easy to add backward-compatible extensions. An earlier specification had a Type of Service metric, so that each type of service could have its own link cost, but that mechanism was never deployed and was later deprecated. This RFC reuses those TOS fields: they are redefined and carry a separate metric for each topology. The differences from the old approach are three. The type of service in the IP header no longer picks the routing table directly, and how traffic is classified is outside the document. Falling back to the default table when a route is missing is now optional. And a link or prefix that is not advertised for a topology simply does not exist in it.

sections.title: The Terms and the Area Rules
sections.content:
A Non-MT router is a router that does not have the MT capability, and an MT router is one that does. The MT-ID is the renamed TOS field in the link state advertisements, now standing for Multi-Topology ID. The default topology is the topology built using the TOS 0 metric, and an MT topology is one built using the corresponding MT-ID metric. A Non-MT-Area is an area that contains only non-MT routers, and an MT-Area is an area that contains both non-MT routers and MT routers, or only MT routers.

Each OSPF interface belongs to a single area, and all the MTs sharing that link need to belong to the same area. The area boundaries for all MTs are therefore the same, but each MT's attachment to the area is independent. Each interface can be configured to belong to a set of topologies, and a single adjacency is formed with the neighbours on the interface even when the interface takes part in multiple topologies. Adjacency formation is independent of the topologies configured on the local interface and on the neighbouring router.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC names the pieces. A Non-MT router has no multi-topology capability, an MT router does. The MT-ID is the TOS field in the link state advertisements, renamed to stand for a topology number. The default topology is the one built with the TOS 0 metric, and an MT topology is the one built with the metric for its own MT-ID. A Non-MT-Area holds only non-MT routers; an MT-Area holds a mix of MT and non-MT routers, or only MT routers. Each OSPF interface belongs to a single area, and all the topologies sharing that link belong to the same area, so the area boundaries are the same for every topology while each topology attaches to the area independently.

sections.title: Advertising Metrics and Computing Paths
sections.content:
The TOS metric field is reused to advertise the topology specific metric for links and prefixes belonging to that topology. The TOS field is redefined as the MT-ID in the payload of Router, Summary, and Type-5 and Type-7 AS-external link state advertisements. MT-ID metrics in the link state advertisements SHOULD be in ascending order of MT-ID, and if an MT-ID exists in an advertisement or router link multiple times, the metric in the first MT-ID instance MUST be used.

When a router establishes a full adjacency over a link that belongs to a set of topologies, it advertises the corresponding cost for each MT-ID. By default all links are included in the default topology, and all advertised prefixes belonging to the default topology use the TOS 0 metric. Each MT has its own MT-ID metric field, and when a link is not part of a given MT the corresponding MT-ID metric is excluded from the advertisement. The Network-LSA does not contain any MT information, because the designated router is shared by all the MTs, so there is no change to it. In Summary-LSAs and Type-5 and Type-7 AS-external-LSAs, the TOS metric fields are redefined as MT-ID metric fields and are used to advertise prefix and router reachability in the corresponding topology.

When a link or prefix that existed or was reachable in a certain topology is no longer part of that topology, or is unreachable in it, a new version of the link state advertisement MUST be originated, excluding the metric information representing the link or prefix in that topology. The MT metric in the Router-LSA can also be set to the maximum possible metric to enable the router to become a stub in a certain topology.

By considering the MT-ID metrics, OSPF computes multiple topologies and finds paths to IP prefixes for each MT independently: a separate SPF is computed for each MT-ID. Network-LSAs are used by all topologies during the computation, but during the SPF for a given MT-ID only the links and metrics for that MT-ID are considered, and the entries in the router routing table are also MT-ID specific.

Since AS-External-LSAs use the high-order bit in the MT-ID field for the external metric type, only MT-IDs in the range 0 to 127 are valid. The reserved values are 0 for the metric associated with the default topology, 1 for the default multicast topology, 2 for IPv4 in-band management purposes, 3 to 31 for assignments by IANA, 32 to 127 for development, experimental and proprietary features, and 128 to 255 are invalid and SHOULD be ignored.

It is outside the scope of the document to specify how the information in the topology specific forwarding structures is used during packet forwarding, or how incoming packets are associated with the corresponding topology. For correct operation, both the forwarding behaviour and the methods of associating incoming packets with a topology must be applied consistently in the network.
sections.plainLanguage: One adjacency is formed with the neighbours on an interface, even when the interface takes part in several topologies. When a router forms a full adjacency over a link, it advertises the cost for each topology in turn, and a link that is not part of a topology leaves that topology's metric out. The Network-LSA is unchanged, because the designated router is shared by all topologies. Each router computes a separate shortest path tree for each topology, using only that topology's links and metrics, and its routing table entries are per topology.

sections.title: Holding Links Out of the Default Topology
sections.content:
The Multi-Topologies imply that all the routers participate in the default topology. However, it can be useful to exclude some links from the default topology and reserve them for some specific classes of traffic.

OSPF does not have the notion of an unreachable link: all links can have a maximum metric of 0xFFFF advertised in the Router-LSA. The link exclusion capability therefore requires routers to ignore the TOS 0 metrics in Router-LSAs in the default topology and to alternately use the MT-ID#0 metric to advertise the metric associated with the default topology. All routers within an area MUST agree on how the metric for the default topology will be advertised. The unused T-bit is defined as the MT-bit in the option field, in order to ensure that a Multi-Topology link-excluding capable router will only form an adjacency with another similarly configured router. If the capability is enabled, the MT-bit MUST be set in Hello packets and SHOULD be set in Database Description packets.

A new parameter in the Area Data Structure, DefaultExclusionCapability, ensures that all routers in an area have this capability enabled before the default topology can be disabled on a router link in the area without causing backward-compatibility problems. When an area data structure is created the parameter is disabled by default. While it is disabled, the MT-bit MUST be cleared in Hello packets, and a link that participates in a non-default topology is automatically included in the default topology to support backward compatibility with non-MT routers. When the capability is enabled, the router will only accept a Hello packet if the MT-bit is set.

Disabling the default topology on an interface does not affect the installation of connected routes for the interface in the default topology; it only affects what the router advertises in its Router-LSA. This allows OSPF control packets to be sent and received over an interface even if the default topology is disabled on it.

When the capability is enabled and the link does not participate in the default topology, the MT-ID#0 metric is not advertised and the link's TOS 0 metric is ignored during the default topology SPF computation. When the capability is enabled and the link does participate in the default topology, the MT-ID#0 metric is used to advertise the metric associated with the default topology. Independently of the capability, the TOS 0 metric is used for Summary-LSAs and Type-5 and Type-7 AS-external-LSAs: if the prefix or router does not exist in the default topology the TOS 0 metric is set to infinity, 0xFFFFFF, and if it does exist the TOS 0 metric is used to advertise the metric in the default topology.
sections.plainLanguage: Some links may be held out of the default topology and reserved for particular traffic. OSPF has no notion of an unreachable link, so the way to do this is a capability called DefaultExclusionCapability, which makes the routers ignore the TOS 0 metric in Router-LSAs and use the metric for MT-ID 0 instead. A previously unused bit in the OSPF options, the MT-bit, is set in Hello packets so that a router only forms an adjacency with another router that has the same capability. The capability is off by default, and turning it on is what allows a link to leave the default topology. It does not stop OSPF control packets from being sent over that link.

sections.title: Living with Routers That Do Not Know
sections.content:
The default metric field is mandatory in all link state advertisements, even when the metric value is 0. Even when a link or prefix does not exist in the default topology, a non-MT router will consider the zero value in the metric field as a valid metric and consider the link or prefix as part of the default topology.

To prevent that, an MT-capable router will include all links as part of the default topology. If links need to be removed from the default topology, an MT-capable router must be configured in DefaultExclusionCapability mode. In this mode, routers ensure that all other routers in the area are in that mode before considering the MT-ID#0 metric in the SPF calculation. Only then can the TOS 0 metric field in Router-LSAs be safely ignored during the default topology SPF computation.

For any prefix or router to become reachable in a certain topology, a contiguous path inside that topology must exist between the calculating router and the destination prefix or router.

A change to an area's DefaultExclusionCapability requires additional processing for area neighbours that are suppressing Hello packets. When the capability for an area is changed, Hello suppression must be disabled for these neighbours for a period of RouterDeadInterval seconds, with the Hello packets sent with the DC-bit clear during that period. After that time, either the adjacency is taken down because of the rejection of Hello packets with a conflicting MT-bit, or Hello suppression is renegotiated.

Introducing MT-OSPF into a network can be done gradually, so that MT routers and non-MT routers participate in the default topology while the MT routers participate in other topologies. The RFC sets out a migration: part of an area is upgraded to be MT capable, and the MT routers interact with the non-MT routers in the default topology while taking part in other topologies as required. If a new non-backbone area is created for the MT routers, it may be configured in DefaultExclusionCapability mode straight away, since there is no interaction required with non-MT routers, and in that mode the default topology can be excluded on links as required. If there are several non-backbone areas where MT is being used, it is desirable that the backbone area first be upgraded to be MT capable, so that inter-area routing is ensured for MT destinations in different areas. Gradually, the whole network can be made MT capable. Inter-area routing for the MT-area still depends on the backbone area, so if different areas configured for a given topology need to communicate, the backbone area also needs to be configured for that topology.
sections.plainLanguage: A non-MT router treats the zero value in the metric field as a valid metric, so it will consider any link or prefix as part of the default topology even when the MT-capable router has left it out. To avoid that, an MT-capable router includes all links in the default topology unless it is configured in DefaultExclusionCapability mode, in which case it waits until every other router in the area is in that mode before it ignores the TOS 0 metric. Migration is gradual: part of an area is upgraded first, a new non-backbone area for the MT routers can be created directly in the capability mode, the backbone area should be upgraded next so that inter-area routing works for the new topologies, and finally the whole network becomes MT capable.

sections.title: Reaching the Routers for Management
sections.content:
When multiple OSPF topologies exist within a domain, some of the routers can be configured to participate in a subset of the topologies in the network. The RFC describes two options for enabling operations staff or network management stations to access those routers.

The first is to set up a dedicated management topology, or in-band management topology, which includes all the routers that need to be managed. The computed routes in that topology are installed into the mgmt Routing Information Base. If the mgmt topology uses a set of non-overlapping address space with the default topology, those mgmt routes can also optionally be installed into the default Routing Information Base. The advantages of duplicating the mgmt routes in both tables are that the network management utilities on the system do not have to be modified to use a table other than the default one, and that the mgmt topology can share the same link with the default topology if it is so designed.

The second is to extend the default topology to all the nodes, even in the case where the default topology is not used for IP forwarding on some of them, for the purpose of network management. Operators SHOULD set a high cost on the links that belong to the extended portion of the default topology, so that IP data traffic is not forwarded through those nodes during network topology changes.
sections.plainLanguage: When several topologies exist, some routers may take part in only a subset of them, so operations staff and network management stations need a way to reach those routers. One option is a dedicated management topology that includes every router that has to be managed, with its routes installed in its own routing table, and optionally in the default table as well if the address space does not overlap. The other option is to extend the default topology to the routers that need managing, with a high cost on those links so that ordinary traffic is not sent through them.

sections.title: Security and the Registries
sections.content:
The document does not raise any security issues that are not already covered by the OSPF specification.

For IANA, the T-bit defined in the earlier TOS specification for a router's TOS capability is redefined as the MT-bit in this document, and the TOS field for Router-LSAs, Summary-LSAs, and Type-5 and Type-7 AS-external-LSAs is redefined as the MT-ID. IANA created a new registry, OSPF Multi-Topology ID Values, with the assignments and registration policies listed in the document.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says it raises no security issues beyond those already covered by OSPF. It also records the IANA work: the previously unused T-bit in the OSPF options is redefined as the MT-bit, the TOS field in the Router, Summary and external link state advertisements is redefined as the MT-ID, and IANA created a registry of OSPF Multi-Topology ID Values.

viz.caption: THE MIGRATION STEPS THE RFC SETS OUT

items.title: Upgrade part of an area
items.text: The MT routers interact with the non-MT routers in the default topology and take part in other topologies.

items.title: Create a new area in capability mode
items.text: A new non-backbone area for the MT routers can use DefaultExclusionCapability from the start.

items.title: Upgrade the backbone next
items.text: The backbone should be MT capable first so that inter-area routing works for MT destinations.

items.title: Make the whole network MT capable
items.text: Gradually every router takes part, and the backbone also needs configuring for each topology in use.
